# Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta (MN 140 (PTS MN iii 237))

**ID:** MN 140 (PTS MN iii 237)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Analysis of the Elements
**PTS:** MN iii 237
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn140
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta* (MN 140) is the 140th discourse of the Majjhimanikāya [SuttaCentral]. Set in a potter's workshop, the narrative recounts an overnight encounter between the Buddha and the wanderer Pukkasāti, who is termed a *kulaputta* ('clansman') and had gone forth in dedication to the Buddha without ever having seen him [SuttaCentral; Schopen 1997; Segall 2003; Nattier, Earliest Chinese Buddhist Translations]. Unaware that his companion is the Buddha himself, Pukkasāti receives an exposition analyzing a person into six elements (*dhātu*), six fields of sensory contact, eighteen mental investigations (*upavicāra*), and four foundations or determinations (*adhiṭṭhāna*) [SuttaCentral; Gaffney 2003; Stuart 2012]. The Buddha details the contemplation of both internal bodily aspects (such as earth, water, fire, and wind) and external elements, progressing through space and pure consciousness to the cessation of feelings (*vedanā*) and final peace [Stuart 2012; Anālayo 2014; Melnikova 2014; Wen, Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism]. Recognizing the teacher only after the exposition concludes, Pukkasāti attains realization through personal comprehension rather than blind faith [Segall 2003].

Full parallels are preserved in Chinese in the *Madhyamāgama* (MĀ 162) and as an independent translation (T 511), in Tibetan in the *Upāyikā* (Up 1.041 / D 4094), and in partial canonical correspondences including DN 33, AN 6.1, and SN 35.248 [SuttaCentral; Nattier, Earliest Chinese Buddhist Translations; Anālayo 2014]. While MN 140 and MĀ 162 present the core meeting, T 511 includes narrative background—such as Pukkasāti's previous royal status in Takṣaśīla, his friendship with King Bimbisāra, and the Buddha's foreknowledge of his impending death—that Theravāda tradition preserves in Buddhaghosa's commentary (*Papañcasūdanī*) [Nattier, Earliest Chinese Buddhist Translations; Wu 2012]. Significant textual reuse is shared with the Sanskrit *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra*, the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and Śāntideva's *Śikṣāsamuccaya* [Stuart 2012; Anālayo 2014; DharmaNexus]. In the Pali Canon, DharmaNexus records extensive reuse with element teachings in MN 28, MN 62, and the Abhidhamma *Dhātuvibhaṅga* (Vb 3), reflecting a broader genre of expanded *vibhaṅga* expositions relocated from Saṁyutta topics into the Majjhimanikāya [Wen, Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism; Sujato, History of Mindfulness; DharmaNexus].
